title: Towards an extension of Fault Trees in the Predictive Maintenance Scenario
authors: Roberta De Fazio, Stefano Marrone, Laura Verde, Vincenzo Reccia, Paolo Valletta
text: In the context of Industry 4.0, the Predictive Maintenance (PdM) has gained ground, becoming one of the more interesting applications of Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), from healthcare to railway [1,2,3]. The need to ensure high reliability in critical systems is leading to more precise analysis techniques [4]. Both Model-Based (MB) [5,6] and Data-Driven (DD) [7] approaches have been widely adopted to accomplish these issues. Among MB methods, Fault Trees (FTs) are a solid formalism, widely accepted in both academia and industry. One of the most appreciated results achieved by this formalism is its adaptability to the evolution of systems and analysis processes: different extensions of FT can capture various aspects of the system to model, from repairability to failure sequences. This research has the objective of improving the FT formalism by adapting it to the new challenge of PdM. The long-term goal is to join the benefits of DD techniques (flexibility and adaptability to several contexts) with the transparency and explainability of MB methods. Other possible benefits to demonstrate are the necessity of smaller datasets since the presence of prior knowledge about the context [8,9] traditionally lacks in pure- DD approaches. Last, MB methods are most accepted in critical system validation and certification processes. This problem is emphasized in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs): industrial settings would greatly enjoy the Machine Learning (ML) -based applications, but the capability to inspect a model — as in MB contexts — is of great importance. The possibility of combining the points of strengths of both methods, ensuring better realism and higher interpretability of the results led to propose new hybrid techniques. Few works in the literature, indeed, propose similar approaches. In [7], the authors use a set of mathematical equations as MB technique for evaluating the residuals and classifying the faults by using Bayesian Networks (BNs) while in [10] after computing residuals, the authors use Support Vector Data Description classifier for ranking minimal diagnosis candidates. The approach proposed in [11] provides a hybrid BN, boosted with a symptom layer including nodes with residuals’ features, nodes containing knowledge-based information and nodes composed of data-extracted features. Another approach, proposed in [12], exploits BN formalism trained on faulty data fused with the reference model driven on normal conditions. Some approaches are based on the usage of Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) [13] which is a more powerful formalism than FTs, even if there is a trade-off between expressiveness and usability of formal languages [14]. Some works presenting the usage of DBNs in PdM are: [15], where DBNs are used to learn system observable dynamics, combined with false error correction by the usage of Conditional Probability Table; [16], which relies more on learning algorithms for DBNs, without having an explicit modelling phase; [17], where a BN model is obtained by the merging an Extreme Gradient Boosting approach with prior knowledge embedded into an ontology. One of the most promising bridging techniques between DD and MB is Process Mining (PM). PM is a technique for extracting process models from the real data [18]. To the best of our knowledge, only a few works propose a solution for fault prediction in critical infrastructure via PM [19,20]. This paper proposes the Predictive Fault Tree (PdFT) language, based on State-Event Fault Trees (SEFTs) [21] and Dynamic Fault Trees (DFTs) [22]. The main goal is the improvement of the expressive power of the model itself to allow the design of more complex structures with several behaviours and the evaluation of the performances under these critical behaviours. The language is introduced by defining an abstract syntax, a tentative graphical notation, and some initial considerations about the semantics. This notwithstanding, the proposed formalism is supported by a vision aiming at merging MB and DD approaches; in particular, the usage of three different DD techniques as PM, Time Series Analysis (TSA) and Association Rules Learning (ARL). Concerning this brief review of the state of the art, the original contributions present in this research are: (1) introduction of the PdFT formalism; (2) definition of a usage approach combining MB and DD approaches. The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section II introduces the PdFT formalism while Section III reports a usage scenario of the language, described also by the support of a small example. Section IV ends the paper, reporting the progress of the research and addressing the next steps.
